content_voiceover: This is the etiologic classification of aplastic anemia, and it's worth organizing into acquired versus hereditary causes. Most acquired aplastic anemia is idiopathic and thought to be autoimmune, a T-cell mediated attack on hematopoietic stem cells, which is why immunosuppressive therapy works. Drug causes to remember include NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, certain antibiotics like chloramphenicol, antithyroid drugs, and gold compounds. Toxins include benzene, chlorinated hydrocarbons, and organophosphates. Viral triggers include EBV, parvovirus B19, and seronegative hepatitis, meaning hepatitis that's non-A through non-G, as well as HIV. Other acquired associations include paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria itself, autoimmune and connective tissue disorders such as eosinophilic fasciitis, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus, as well as thymoma, pregnancy, and iatrogenic causes like radiation and cytotoxic chemotherapy. Critically, the diagnosis of aplastic anemia requires you to exclude hypocellular MDS, PNH, large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and lymphoma, since these can all mimic a hypocellular marrow. The hereditary causes, which you must screen for especially in younger patients, are Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.
keypoints: Most acquired AA is idiopathic/autoimmune (T-cell mediated)
Drug triggers: NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antithyroids, gold, chloramphenicol
Must exclude hypocellular MDS, PNH, LGLL, lymphoma before diagnosing AA
Hereditary causes: Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond, CAMT
